claim: The study included 143,390 complete twin pairs born between 1886 and 1994.
source: We conducted an individual-based pooled analysis of 40 twin cohorts including 143,390 complete twin pairs born 1886–1994.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the sample size and birth year range of the study population.

claim: Genetic variance showed a generally increasing trend across birth-year cohorts.
source: Although genetic variance showed a generally increasing trend across the birth-year cohorts, heritability estimates (0.69-0.84 in men and 0.53-0.78 in women) did not present any clear pattern of secular changes.
evidence: The abstract presents findings from the analysis showing trends in genetic variance.

claim: Heritability estimates ranged from 0.69 to 0.84 in men.
source: Although genetic variance showed a generally increasing trend across the birth-year cohorts, heritability estimates (0.69-0.84 in men and 0.53-0.78 in women) did not present any clear pattern of secular changes.
evidence: The abstract provides specific heritability estimates for men derived from the study data.

claim: Heritability estimates ranged from 0.53 to 0.78 in women.
source: Although genetic variance showed a generally increasing trend across the birth-year cohorts, heritability estimates (0.69-0.84 in men and 0.53-0.78 in women) did not present any clear pattern of secular changes.
evidence: The abstract provides specific heritability estimates for women derived from the study data.

claim: Heritability estimates did not present any clear pattern of secular changes across birth-year cohorts.
source: Although genetic variance showed a generally increasing trend across the birth-year cohorts, heritability estimates (0.69-0.84 in men and 0.53-0.78 in women) did not present any clear pattern of secular changes.
evidence: The abstract presents the main finding regarding the lack of clear secular trends in heritability.

claim: Total height variance was greatest in North America and Australia.
source: Comparing geographic-cultural regions (Europe, North America and Australia, and East Asia), total height variance was greatest in North America and Australia and lowest in East Asia, but no clear pattern in the heritability estimates across the birth-year cohorts emerged.
evidence: The abstract reports comparative findings across geographic regions based on the study data.

claim: Total height variance was lowest in East Asia.
source: Comparing geographic-cultural regions (Europe, North America and Australia, and East Asia), total height variance was greatest in North America and Australia and lowest in East Asia, but no clear pattern in the heritability estimates across the birth-year cohorts emerged.
evidence: The abstract reports comparative findings across geographic regions based on the study data.

claim: The findings do not support the hypothesis that heritability of height is lower in populations with low living standards than in affluent populations.
source: Our findings do not support the hypothesis that heritability of height is lower in populations with low living standards than in affluent populations, nor that heritability of height will increase within a population as living standards improve.
evidence: The abstract presents the main conclusion of the study based on the analysis of the data.

claim: The findings do not support the hypothesis that heritability of height will increase within a population as living standards improve.
source: Our findings do not support the hypothesis that heritability of height is lower in populations with low living standards than in affluent populations, nor that heritability of height will increase within a population as living standards improve.
evidence: The abstract presents the main conclusion of the study based on the analysis of the data.

claim: Height is one of the most heritable human quantitative phenotypes.
source: Since the studies of height in the late 19th and early 20th centuries (Galton, 1886; Pearson and Lee, 1903; Fisher, 1919), twin, adoption and family studies have shown that height is one of the most heritable human quantitative phenotypes (Silventoinen, 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites previous research establishing height as highly heritable.

claim: Genetic linkage studies have helped to elucidate the location of genetic effects in the genome for height.
source: More recently, genetic linkage studies have helped to elucidate the location of genetic effects in the genome (Perola et al., 2007) and genome-wide association (GWA) studies allowed identification of loci consistently associated with height in populations of different ancestry (Cho et al., 2009; Hao et al., 2013; Lango Allen et al., 2010; N'Diaye et al., 2011; Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites previous genetic studies on height.

claim: Genome-wide association studies allowed identification of loci consistently associated with height in populations of different ancestry.
source: More recently, genetic linkage studies have helped to elucidate the location of genetic effects in the genome (Perola et al., 2007) and genome-wide association (GWA) studies allowed identification of loci consistently associated with height in populations of different ancestry (Cho et al., 2009; Hao et al., 2013; Lango Allen et al., 2010; N'Diaye et al., 2011; Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites previous GWAS studies on height.

claim: Environmental factors such as nutrition and childhood diseases can affect final attained height.
source: Besides the genetic factors, a multitude of environmental factors, such as nutrition and childhood diseases, operate during the growth period and can affect the final attained height.
evidence: The introduction discusses established knowledge about environmental influences on height.

claim: Proximate biological determinants of height are associated with social and economic conditions and living standards.
source: These and other proximate biological determinants of height are further associated with social and economic conditions, which in turn are associated with living standards (Bozzoli et al., 2009; Bogin, 2001; Eveleth and Tanner, 1990; Steckel, 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites previous research on the relationship between height determinants and socioeconomic factors.

claim: The secular trend of increasing height over the 20th century observed in many parts of the world probably reflects continuous improvement in the standard of living.
source: The secular trend of increasing height over the 20th century observed in many parts of the world, which has slowed or stopped in most northern European countries, probably reflects the continuous improvement in the standard of living (Eveleth and Tanner, 1990; Cole, 2003; Stulp and Barrett, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites previous research on secular trends in height and their interpretation.

claim: The secular trend of increasing height has slowed or stopped in most northern European countries.
source: The secular trend of increasing height over the 20th century observed in many parts of the world, which has slowed or stopped in most northern European countries, probably reflects the continuous improvement in the standard of living (Eveleth and Tanner, 1990; Cole, 2003; Stulp and Barrett, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites previous research on secular trends in height.

claim: The height difference between the tallest and shortest populations a century ago (19–20 cm) has remained the same for women.
source: A recent study showed that the height difference between the tallest and shortest populations a century ago (19–20 cm) has remained the same for women and increased for men (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2016) .
evidence: The introduction cites a recent study on global height differences.

claim: The height difference between the tallest and shortest populations has increased for men over the past century.
source: A recent study showed that the height difference between the tallest and shortest populations a century ago (19–20 cm) has remained the same for women and increased for men (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2016) .
evidence: The introduction cites a recent study on global height differences.

claim: Twin and family studies have consistently estimated that heritability of adult height in general populations is approximately 0.80.
source: Twin and family studies have consistently estimated that the proportion of variation in adult height explained by genetic differences between individuals, or heritability, in general populations is approximately 0.80 (Fisher, 1919; Silventoinen et al., 2003; Stunkard et al., 1986).
evidence: The introduction cites previous twin and family studies on height heritability.

claim: There is a hypothesis that heritability is not constant and can differ in environments having different amounts of environmental variation.
source: There is a hypothesis that heritability is not constant and can differ in environments having different amount of environmental variation.
evidence: The introduction presents a hypothesis that motivates the study.

claim: It has been suggested that heritability of height is lower in populations with low living standards compared with affluent populations since poverty can lead to a lack of basic necessities important for human growth.
source: Accordingly, it has been suggested that heritability of height is lower in populations with low living standards compared with affluent populations since poverty can lead to a lack of basic necessities important for human growth in part of the population (Steckel, 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites a hypothesis from previous literature.

claim: A study in Finnish twins born between 1900 and 1957 showed that the heritability of height increased across birth cohorts born in the first half of the century when the standard of living increased.
source: A study in Finnish twins born between 1900 and 1957 showed that the heritability of height increased across birth cohorts born in the first half of the century when the standard of living increased and leveled off after World War II thus supporting this hypothesis (Silventoinen et al., 2000).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study on heritability changes over time.

claim: The heritability of height in Finnish twins leveled off after World War II.
source: A study in Finnish twins born between 1900 and 1957 showed that the heritability of height increased across birth cohorts born in the first half of the century when the standard of living increased and leveled off after World War II thus supporting this hypothesis (Silventoinen et al., 2000).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study on heritability changes over time.

claim: Mean height was greater in men than in women in the pooled data.
source: In the pooled data (all twin cohorts together), mean height was greater in men than in women and increased over the birth-year cohorts in both sexes; the decrease ( > 1 cm) observed in the latest birth cohort mainly reflects differences in the distribution of different twin cohorts within each group (Table 1).
evidence: The Results section presents descriptive statistics from the study data, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Mean height increased over the birth-year cohorts in both sexes.
source: In the pooled data (all twin cohorts together), mean height was greater in men than in women and increased over the birth-year cohorts in both sexes; the decrease ( > 1 cm) observed in the latest birth cohort mainly reflects differences in the distribution of different twin cohorts within each group (Table 1).
evidence: The Results section presents descriptive statistics from the study data, with reference to Table 1.

claim: The decrease in mean height (>1 cm) observed in the latest birth cohort mainly reflects differences in the distribution of different twin cohorts within each group.
source: In the pooled data (all twin cohorts together), mean height was greater in men than in women and increased over the birth-year cohorts in both sexes; the decrease ( > 1 cm) observed in the latest birth cohort mainly reflects differences in the distribution of different twin cohorts within each group (Table 1).
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the observed pattern in the data.

claim: Both means and variances of height were significantly different between twin cohorts in all birth-year and sex groups.
source: Both means and variances were significantly different between twin cohorts in all birth-year and sex groups.
evidence: The Results section reports statistical test results from the study data.

claim: Mean height was shorter in East Asia than in Europe and North America and Australia in all birth-year and sex groups.
source: Mean height was shorter in East Asia than in Europe and North America and Australia in all birth-year and sex groups.
evidence: The Results section presents comparative findings across geographic regions from the study data.

claim: The increase in mean height over the birth cohorts (from 1940–1949 to 1980–1994) was substantially greater in East Asia than in the other two geographic-cultural regions.
source: The increase in mean height over the birth cohorts (from 1940–1949 to 1980–1994) was substantially greater in East Asia than in the other two geographic-cultural regions.
evidence: The Results section presents comparative findings across geographic regions from the study data.

claim: The variance of height was generally greater in men than in women.
source: The variance of height was generally greater in men than in women, lowest in East Asia and greatest in North America and Australia, and showed a general trend to increase over the birth cohorts.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on height variance from the study data.

claim: The variance of height was lowest in East Asia and greatest in North America and Australia.
source: The variance of height was generally greater in men than in women, lowest in East Asia and greatest in North America and Australia, and showed a general trend to increase over the birth cohorts.
evidence: The Results section presents comparative findings across geographic regions from the study data.

claim: The variance of height showed a general trend to increase over the birth cohorts.
source: The variance of height was generally greater in men than in women, lowest in East Asia and greatest in North America and Australia, and showed a general trend to increase over the birth cohorts.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on temporal trends in height variance from the study data.

claim: In men, there was a trend for an increasing total variance from birth cohort 1940–1949 onwards.
source: In men, there was a trend for an increasing total variance from birth cohort 1940–1949 onwards; genetic variance also increased during this period but especially in the two latest birth-year cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994).
evidence: The Results section presents findings on variance components from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In men, genetic variance increased from birth cohort 1940–1949 onwards, especially in the two latest birth-year cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994).
source: In men, there was a trend for an increasing total variance from birth cohort 1940–1949 onwards; genetic variance also increased during this period but especially in the two latest birth-year cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994).
evidence: The Results section presents findings on genetic variance from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In men, height variance due to the environment shared by co-twins was significant from birth cohorts 1920–1929 to 1970–1979.
source: Height variance due to the environment shared by co-twins was significant from birth cohorts 1920–1929 to 1970–1979, being greatest from 1950 to 1969.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on shared environmental variance from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In men, shared environmental variance was greatest from 1950 to 1969.
source: Height variance due to the environment shared by co-twins was significant from birth cohorts 1920–1929 to 1970–1979, being greatest from 1950 to 1969.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on shared environmental variance from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In men, the effect of environmental factors unique to each twin individual including measurement error was more similar across birth-year cohorts.
source: The effect of environmental factors unique to each twin individual including measurement error was more similar across birth-year cohorts.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on unique environmental variance from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In men, heritability estimates were greatest in the two earliest and the two latest birth-year cohorts.
source: Heritability estimates ranged from 0.69 to 0.84 and were greatest in the two earliest and the two latest birth-year cohorts (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section presents findings on heritability from the study data, with reference to Table 2.

claim: In women, the total variance started to increase from birth cohort 1940–1949.
source: In women, although the total variance also started to increase from birth cohort 1940–1949, genetic variance showed an increasing trend from the earliest birth-year cohort.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on variance components in women from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In women, genetic variance showed an increasing trend from the earliest birth-year cohort.
source: In women, although the total variance also started to increase from birth cohort 1940–1949, genetic variance showed an increasing trend from the earliest birth-year cohort.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on genetic variance in women from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In women, both shared and unique environmental factors explained variation in height in all analyzed birth-year cohorts.
source: Both shared and unique environmental factors explained variation in height in all analyzed birth-year cohorts; whereas the shared environmental variance was somewhat greater in the latest cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994) unique environmental variance was greatest in the earliest one.

claim: In women, shared environmental variance was somewhat greater in the latest cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994).
source: Both shared and unique environmental factors explained variation in height in all analyzed birth-year cohorts; whereas the shared environmental variance was somewhat greater in the latest cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994) unique environmental variance was greatest in the earliest one.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on shared environmental variance in women from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In women, unique environmental variance was greatest in the earliest birth-year cohort.
source: Both shared and unique environmental factors explained variation in height in all analyzed birth-year cohorts; whereas the shared environmental variance was somewhat greater in the latest cohorts (1970–1979 and 1980–1994) unique environmental variance was greatest in the earliest one.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on unique environmental variance in women from the study data, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The variance components differed between sexes in all birth-year cohorts.
source: Although the variance components differed between sexes in all birth-year cohorts, the relative contribution of the genetic and environmental variance components did not differ by sex from 1930–1939 to 1960–1969 (Supplementary file1B).
evidence: The Results section presents findings on sex differences in variance components from the study data.

claim: The relative contribution of the genetic and environmental variance components did not differ by sex from 1930–1939 to 1960–1969.
source: Although the variance components differed between sexes in all birth-year cohorts, the relative contribution of the genetic and environmental variance components did not differ by sex from 1930–1939 to 1960–1969 (Supplementary file1B).
evidence: The Results section presents findings on sex differences in relative variance components from the study data.

claim: In women, heritability estimates were lowest in the earliest and latest cohorts, particularly in 1886–1909.
source: In contrast to the results in men, heritability estimates in women (0.53 to 0.78) were lowest in the earliest and latest cohorts, particularly in 1886–1909.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on heritability in women from the study data, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The interaction effect of birth year on the genetic path coefficient was 0.050 (95% CI 0.018–0.082) in men per 10 years.
source: When we studied the effect of birth year on the genetic variance by using gene-environment interaction models, modest but statistically significant increase was found. The interaction effect was 0.050 (95% CI 0.018–0.082) in men and 0.043 (95% CI 0.019–0.071) in women for the genetic path coefficient per 10 years.
evidence: The Results section presents findings from gene-environment interaction modeling.

claim: The interaction effect of birth year on the genetic path coefficient was 0.043 (95% CI 0.019–0.071) in women per 10 years.
source: When we studied the effect of birth year on the genetic variance by using gene-environment interaction models, modest but statistically significant increase was found. The interaction effect was 0.050 (95% CI 0.018–0.082) in men and 0.043 (95% CI 0.019–0.071) in women for the genetic path coefficient per 10 years.
evidence: The Results section presents findings from gene-environment interaction modeling.

claim: The genetic variance increased by 1.37 (95% CI 0.50–2.27) in men per 25 years.
source: This turns to 1.37 (95% CI 0.50–2.27) increase of genetic variance in men and 1.07 (95% CI 0.46–1.79) increase of genetic variance in women per 25 years, i.e. approximately one human generation.

claim: The genetic variance increased by 1.07 (95% CI 0.46–1.79) in women per 25 years.
source: This turns to 1.37 (95% CI 0.50–2.27) increase of genetic variance in men and 1.07 (95% CI 0.46–1.79) increase of genetic variance in women per 25 years, i.e. approximately one human generation.
evidence: The Results section presents findings from gene-environment interaction modeling converted to a 25-year timeframe.

claim: The pattern of genetic and environmental variances in Europe was practically the same as that observed for the pooled data.
source: The pattern in Europe was practically the same as that observed for the pooled data because it represents a large proportion of the total sample.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on regional patterns with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In North America and Australia, the total variance of height was greater than in Europe.
source: In North America and Australia, the total variance of height was greater than in Europe, but the pattern of genetic and environmental variances was less consistent across birth-year cohorts.
evidence: The Results section presents comparative findings across geographic regions with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In North America and Australia, the pattern of genetic and environmental variances was less consistent across birth-year cohorts than in Europe.
source: In North America and Australia, the total variance of height was greater than in Europe, but the pattern of genetic and environmental variances was less consistent across birth-year cohorts.
evidence: The Results section presents comparative findings across geographic regions with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In East Asia, the magnitude of the variance components between the birth-year cohorts fluctuated more than in the other two geographic-cultural regions due to smaller sample size.
source: In East Asia, because of the smaller sample size, the magnitude of the variance components between the birth-year cohorts fluctuated more than in the other two geographic-cultural regions.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on East Asian data with reference to Figure 1 and provides an explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Genetic variance was generally greater in men than in women in the three geographic-cultural regions.
source: Genetic variance was generally greater in men than in women in the three geographic-cultural regions.
evidence: The Results section presents findings on sex differences in genetic variance across regions with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Infant mortality rates are higher in men than in women, both in singletons and twins.
source: Since infant mortality rates are higher in men than in women, both in singletons (Drevenstedt et al., 2008) and twins (Pongou, 2013), the higher heritability observed for men in the earliest cohorts could be explained by selection effects since those who survived were the genetically more advantaged and thus less vulnerable to environmental conditions.
evidence: The Discussion cites previous research on infant mortality rates.

claim: The higher heritability observed for men in the earliest cohorts could be explained by selection effects since those who survived were the genetically more advantaged and thus less vulnerable to environmental conditions.
source: Since infant mortality rates are higher in men than in women, both in singletons (Drevenstedt et al., 2008) and twins (Pongou, 2013), the higher heritability observed for men in the earliest cohorts could be explained by selection effects since those who survived were the genetically more advantaged and thus less vulnerable to environmental conditions.
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the study findings based on cited research and logical inference.

claim: The greater relative environmental effect on height variation in women than in men is in agreement with findings in Finnish twins born prior to 1958.
source: The greater relative environmental effect on height variation in women than in men, although unexpected because women's growth is considered to be more resistant to environmental influences, is in agreement with the findings in Finnish twins born prior to 1958 (Silventoinen et al., 2000).
evidence: The Discussion compares the study findings with previous research.

claim: Women's growth is considered to be more resistant to environmental influences.
source: The greater relative environmental effect on height variation in women than in men, although unexpected because women's growth is considered to be more resistant to environmental influences, is in agreement with the findings in Finnish twins born prior to 1958 (Silventoinen et al., 2000).
evidence: The Discussion references established knowledge about sex differences in growth.

claim: The greater environmental effect on height in women might indicate differential access to food and medical care.
source: This might indicate differential access to food and medical care (Eveleth and Tanner, 1990).
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative interpretation of the findings with citation support.

claim: Women are more likely to develop osteoporosis leading to shrinking in old age.
source: Women are also more likely to develop osteoporosis leading to shrinking in old age (National Institute of Arthritis and musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, 2014), which may affect the greater influence of unique environmental factors in women born in 1886–1910.
evidence: The Discussion cites established medical knowledge about osteoporosis.

claim: Osteoporosis may affect the greater influence of unique environmental factors in women born in 1886–1910.
source: Women are also more likely to develop osteoporosis leading to shrinking in old age (National Institute of Arthritis and musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, 2014), which may affect the greater influence of unique environmental factors in women born in 1886–1910.
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative interpretation of the study findings.

claim: Genetic factors play an important role in bone loss in early postmenopausal women, but their effect weakens with age and completely disappears with advanced aging.
source: This idea is supported by results showing that although genetic factors play an important role in bone loss in early postmenopausal women, their effect weakens with age and completely disappears with advanced aging (Moayyeri et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion cites previous research on genetic factors in bone loss.

claim: Part of the increase in total variance in some birth-year cohorts was due to the increase in shared environmental variance.
source: However, part of the increase in total variance in some birth-year cohorts was also due to the increase in shared environmental variance.
evidence: The Discussion interprets the study findings on variance components.

claim: Both greater ethnic diversity and variation in living standards have contributed to the secular increase in height variation.
source: This suggests that both greater ethnic diversity and variation in living standards have contributed to the secular increase in height variation.
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the study findings.

claim: Many independent loci contribute to population genetic differences in height and account for 24% of the captured additive genetic variance across 14 European countries.
source: A recent study across 14 European countries found that many independent loci contribute to population genetic differences in height and estimated that these differences account for 24% of the captured additive genetic variance (Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion cites a recent genetic study on height variation.

claim: Both allelic frequencies and the effects of genes affecting height may vary between geographic-cultural regions.
source: Therefore, it may be that both allelic frequencies and the effects of genes affecting height vary between the geographic-cultural regions.
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative interpretation based on cited research.

claim: When the total variance of height was greater in Western populations than in East Asian populations, heritability estimates were largely similar in adolescence.
source: It has been previously shown that even when the total variance of height was greater in Western populations than in East Asian populations, heritability estimates were largely similar in adolescence (Hur et al., 2008) and from 1 to 19 years of age (Jelenkovic et al., 2016); however, the limited statistical power in the data from East Asia does not allow for comparisons across birth cohorts.
evidence: The Discussion cites previous research on height heritability across populations.

claim: Heritability estimates of height were largely similar between Western and East Asian populations from 1 to 19 years of age.
source: It has been previously shown that even when the total variance of height was greater in Western populations than in East Asian populations, heritability estimates were largely similar in adolescence (Hur et al., 2008) and from 1 to 19 years of age (Jelenkovic et al., 2016); however, the limited statistical power in the data from East Asia does not allow for comparisons across birth cohorts.
evidence: The Discussion cites previous research on height heritability across populations.

claim: The limited statistical power in the data from East Asia does not allow for comparisons across birth cohorts.
source: It has been previously shown that even when the total variance of height was greater in Western populations than in East Asian populations, heritability estimates were largely similar in adolescence (Hur et al., 2008) and from 1 to 19 years of age (Jelenkovic et al., 2016); however, the limited statistical power in the data from East Asia does not allow for comparisons across birth cohorts.
evidence: The Discussion acknowledges a limitation of the study regarding East Asian data.

claim: The study has a very large sample size from a multinational database of twin cohorts with adult height data from individuals born between 1886 and 1994.
source: The main strength of the present study is the very large sample size of our multinational database of twin cohorts, with adult height data from individuals born between year 1886 and 1994, allowing a more detailed investigation of the genetic and environmental contributions to individual differences in height across birth cohorts than in the previous studies.

claim: Individual-based data provide improved opportunities for statistical modeling and lack of publication bias.
source: Important advantages of individual-based data are improved opportunities for statistical modeling and lack of publication bias.

claim: Literature-based meta-analyses are difficult for this type of analysis because most published studies do not provide the needed statistics by birth-year cohorts.
source: This type of analysis is difficult to perform by using literature-based meta-analyses because most of the published studies do not provide the needed statistics by birth-year cohorts.

claim: Countries and/or ethnic-cultural regions are not equally represented in the database.
source: However, our study also has limitations. Countries and/or ethnic-cultural regions are not equally represented and the database is heavily weighted toward populations following Westernized lifestyles.

source: In our database, we do not have information on parental height and thus could not take into account assortative mating, which may thus explain part of the shared environmental variation.

claim: Self-reported height may bias analyses toward higher estimates of unique environmental effects due to increased measurement error.

evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of a potential bias from self-reported data.

claim: Variance components estimates should not be affected by changes in the proportion of MZ to DZ twins across birth-year cohorts.

source: Since individuals in longitudinal studies have more than one measurement over time, analyses were restricted to one observation per individual resulting in 323,491 individuals.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the data handling procedures.

claim: After excluding unmatched pairs, the study had 286,780 twin individuals (143,390 complete twin pairs).
source: After excluding unmatched pairs (without data on their co-twins), we had 286,780 twin individuals (143,390 complete twin pairs) born between year 1886 and 1994 (40% monozygotic (MZ), 41% same- sex dizygotic (SSDZ) and 19% opposite-sex dizygotic (OSDZ) twin pairs).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the final sample composition.

claim: The sample consisted of 40% monozygotic (MZ), 41% same-sex dizygotic (SSDZ) and 19% opposite-sex dizygotic (OSDZ) twin pairs.
source: After excluding unmatched pairs (without data on their co-twins), we had 286,780 twin individuals (143,390 complete twin pairs) born between year 1886 and 1994 (40% monozygotic (MZ), 41% same- sex dizygotic (SSDZ) and 19% opposite-sex dizygotic (OSDZ) twin pairs).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the zygosity distribution in the sample.

claim: The smaller proportion of OSDZ compared to SSDZ twins is explained by the fact that some twin cohorts collected only SSDZ twins by design.
source: The smaller proportion of OSDZ compared to SSDZ twins in this study is explained by the fact that some of the twin cohorts in our database have collected, by design, only SSDZ twins and thus do not have data on OSDZ twins.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explains the zygosity distribution.

claim: Cohorts were grouped into three geographical-cultural regions: Europe (18 cohorts), North America and Australia (14 cohorts) and East Asia (six cohorts).
source: In order to analyze possible ethnic-cultural differences in the genetic and environmental contribution on height, cohorts were grouped in three geographical-cultural regions: Europe (18 cohorts), North America and Australia (14 cohorts) and East Asia (six cohorts) with 87,116, 53,359 and 1793 twin pairs, respectively.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the regional grouping of cohorts.

claim: Europe had 87,116 twin pairs, North America and Australia had 53,359 twin pairs, and East Asia had 1,793 twin pairs.
source: In order to analyze possible ethnic-cultural differences in the genetic and environmental contribution on height, cohorts were grouped in three geographical-cultural regions: Europe (18 cohorts), North America and Australia (14 cohorts) and East Asia (six cohorts) with 87,116, 53,359 and 1793 twin pairs, respectively.
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides the sample sizes for each geographic region.

claim: One cohort from the Middle-East and one from South-Asia were not included in sub-analyses by geographic-cultural region because the data were too sparse.
source: One cohort from the Middle-East and the one from South-Asia were not included in these sub-analyses by geographic-cultural region because the data were too sparse to study these two areas separately.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explains the exclusion of certain cohorts from regional analyses.

claim: A Welch's ANOVA was performed showing that means were significantly different between twin cohorts in all sex and birth-year groups.
source: Since the Levene´s test for homogeneity indicated that variances were not homogeneous, a Welch's ANOVA was performed showing that means were significantly different between twin cohorts in all sex and birth-year groups.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the statistical tests performed and their results.

claim: Classic twin modeling is based on linear structural equations.
source: To analyze genetic and environmental influences on the variation of height, we used classic twin modeling based on linear structural equations (Neale and Cardon, 1992).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the analytical approach with citation.

claim: MZ twins share the same genomic sequence, whereas DZ twins share, on average, 50% of their genes identical-by-descent.
source: MZ twins share the same genomic sequence, whereas DZ twins share, on average, 50% of their genes identical-by-descent.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the genetic basis of twin modeling.

claim: It is possible to divide the total variance of height into variance due to additive genetic effects (A), dominance genetic effects (D), common environmental effects (C), and unique environmental effects (E).
source: On this basis, it is possible to divide the total variance of height into variance due to additive genetic effects (A: correlated 1.0 for MZ and 0.5 for DZ pairs), dominance genetic effects (D: 1.0 for MZ and 0.25 for DZ pairs), common (shared) environmental effects (C: by definition, correlated 1.0 for MZ and DZ pairs) and unique (non-shared) environmental effects (E: by definition, uncorrelated in MZ and DZ pairs).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the variance decomposition in twin modeling.

claim: Shared environmental and dominance genetic effects cannot be simultaneously estimated in twins reared together.
source: However, since our data included only twins reared together, we cannot simultaneously estimate shared environmental and dominance genetic effects.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes a limitation of the twin design.

claim: All genetic models were fitted using the OpenMx package (version 2.0.1) in the R statistical platform using the maximum likelihood method.
source: All genetic models were fitted by the OpenMx package (version 2.0.1) in the R statistical platform (Boker et al., 2011) using the maximum likelihood method.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the software and methods used for analysis.

claim: Height values were adjusted for the year of birth and twin cohort within each birth year and sex groups using linear regressions.
source: Prior to conducting the modeling, height values were adjusted for the year of birth and twin cohort within each birth year and sex groups using linear regressions, and the resulting residuals were used as input phenotypes.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the data preprocessing procedures.

claim: The ACE sex-limitation model was selected as a starting point based on MZ correlations being clearly higher than DZ correlations, the magnitude of the difference between MZ and DZ correlations indicating common environmental effects, and lower OSDZ than SSDZ correlations suggesting sex-specific genetic effects.
source: The ACE sex-limitation model was selected as a starting point of the univariate modeling based on the following criteria: (i) MZ within-pair correlations were clearly higher than DZ correlations consistent with the influence of genetic effects, (ii) the magnitude of the difference between MZ and DZ correlations (rDZ > 1/2 rMZ) indicated the presence of common environmental effects and (iii) the lower within-pair correlations for OSDZ than for SSDZ twins observed for most birth-year groups suggested the presence of sex-specific genetic effects (results not shown).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explains the rationale for model selection based on the data.

claim: Both male and female DZ twins are slightly taller than MZ twins in these age groups.
source: Previous findings from this international database showed that both male and female DZ twins are slightly taller than MZ twins in these age groups (Jelenkovic et al., 2015), and thus different means for MZ and DZ twins were allowed.
evidence: The Materials and methods section cites a previous finding from the same database.

claim: Different means for MZ and DZ twins were allowed in the modeling.
source: Previous findings from this international database showed that both male and female DZ twins are slightly taller than MZ twins in these age groups (Jelenkovic et al., 2015), and thus different means for MZ and DZ twins were allowed.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes a modeling decision based on previous findings.

claim: The equal-environment assumption was tested by comparing the ACE model to the saturated model.
source: In the present study, the equal-environment assumption was tested by comparing the ACE model to the saturated model.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes a test of a key assumption in twin modeling.

claim: The fit of the models after Bonferroni correction did not worsen for most birth-year groups, suggesting that the assumption of equality of variances between MZ and DZ twins was not violated.
source: The fit of the models after Bonferroni correction of multiple testing did not worsen for most birth-year groups, which suggested that the assumption of equality of variances between MZ and DZ twins was not violated.
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports the results of assumption testing.

claim: When fixing A, C and E parameters to be the same in men and women, the fit of the model was poorer in all birth-year groups (p<0.0001), suggesting that these variance components differ between sexes.
source: When fixing A, C and E parameters to be the same in men and women, the fit of the model was poorer in all birth-year groups (p<0.0001), suggesting that these variance components differ between sexes.
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports the results of model comparison testing.

claim: A scale model allowing for different sizes of variance components but fixing the relative size to be equal showed statistically significant differences (p<0.0001) in some birth-year cohorts.
source: We additionally fitted a scale model allowing for different sizes of variance components but fixing the relative size of these components to be equal. Since this model also showed statistically significant differences (p<0.0001) in some birth-year cohorts, we decided to present the results separately for men and women.
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports the results of additional model testing.

claim: Sex-specific genetic effects were significant for some birth-year cohorts.
source: Sex-specific genetic effects were significant for some birth-year cohorts, and thus all modeling results are presented in sex-limited form for consistency.
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports findings that influenced the presentation of results.

claim: Comparative model fitting revealed that the C parameter could not be excluded from the model without a significant deterioration in fit.
source: Comparative model fitting revealed that the C parameter could be not excluded from the model without a significant deterioration in fit.
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports the results of model comparison.

claim: Gene-environment interaction modeling was conducted using birth year as an environmental modification factor.
source: In order to study how birth year modifies the genetic and environmental variances of height, we additionally conducted gene-environment interaction modeling using birth year as an environmental modification factor (Purcell, 2002).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes an additional analysis with citation.
